newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's S. Prairies still seen dry - soil scientist.
newsitem.headline: Canada's S. Prairies still seen dry - soil scientist.

text.p: Large parts of Canada's south Prairies were still considered dry or very dry despite rains last week, an Environment Canada soil scientist said.

"Some parts of the Prairies got an inch of rain last week but to put that in perspective, if the soil on average can hold 200 mm (7.9 inches) in the top metre (3 ft 3 in), even if you get an inch of rain that's only 10 percent of the capacity of the soil to hold," said Rick Raddatz, soil scientist with Environment Canada.
The Canadian Wheat Board on June 11 reduced its wheat yield outlook by 0.5 bushels an acre due to dry conditions.
Typical yields on Prairie wheat ranges from 30 to 32 bu/ac but the CWB cut them June 11 to 29.5 to 31.5 bu/ac.
Spring wheat should enter the heading stage in a week. That's when the cereal's need for water is most acute.
A triangular area from Calgary to Lethbridge to Empress, Alberta, was rated very dry with the soil holding less than 30 percent of its optimum moisture capacity, Raddatz said.
All of southern Saskatchewan except for the southwestern districts around Maple Creek were rated dry with the soil holding less than 60 percent of optimum moisture capacity.
Southwest Manitoba was also rated dry, Raddatz added.
Soil moisture data was drawn from 160 Prairie stations on Monday June 23.
